article_title: Too Scared to Learn? The Academic Consequences of Feeling Unsafe in the Classroom
citation: Johanna Lacoe. (2020). Too Scared to Learn? The Academic Consequences of Feeling Unsafe in the Classroom. Urban Education, vol. 55, issue 10. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Treat a safe classroom environment as a prerequisite for productive learning
description: The article opens from the position that "a safe environment is a prerequisite for productive learning," and its empirical finding of a consistent negative relationship between feeling unsafe and test scores grounds this principle. It implies that efforts to improve achievement in middle schools should attend to students' feelings of safety in the classroom.
requirements: Schools need a way to measure students' reported feelings of safety, such as annual student surveys
constraints: The supporting evidence is an observational relationship, not a tested intervention
target_learners: middle school students
examples: The study analyzed survey-reported feelings of safety alongside test scores for more than 340,000 students annually

article_title: CASEL SEL Framework
citation: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL). (2020). What Is SEL? https://casel.org/fundamentals-of-sel/
title: SAFE: four elements of high-quality SEL instruction
description: SAFE is an acronym for four elements the page says characterize high-quality SEL instruction: "Sequenced – following a coordinated set of training approaches to foster the development of competencies; Active – emphasizing active forms of learning to help students practice and master new skills; Focused – implementing curriculum that intentionally emphasizes the development of SEL competencies; and Explicit – defining and targeting specific skills, attitudes, and knowledge." It functions as a design checklist for SEL curricula.
requirements: Curricula must be sequenced, active, focused, and explicit to count as high-quality SEL instruction
constraints: The page presents SAFE as a program-design feature associated with effective SEL programs, not as a tested manipulation in this source
target_learners: K-12 students in classroom SEL instruction
key_sources: Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL). (2020). What Is SEL? https://casel.org/fundamentals-of-sel/

article_title: Identifying Indicators to Support Educational Attainment for Different Groups of English Learners in High School
citation: Allensworth, E.M., de la Torre, M., Franklin, K., & Xu, J. (2025). Identifying Indicators to Support Educational Attainment for Different Groups of English Learners in High School. (Working Paper). Providence, RI: Annenberg EdExchange. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1241
title: Use the same early warning and college readiness indicator systems for English Learners as for other students, but apply group-specific risk thresholds, especially for active English Learners in high school
description: The study concludes that schools can run one early warning and college readiness indicator system for everyone, because "the best indicators are the same for most students"; what differs is the threshold at which students become at risk. For example, active English Learners need attendance above 95% to be very likely to graduate, while former and never English Learners need 90% or higher. Applying group-specific thresholds lets schools use existing systems to identify at-risk English Learners accurately.
requirements: Schools must track GPA, attendance, and course failure data for all students, including English Learner subgroups.
constraints: Thresholds differ for active English Learners in high school, and outcomes were harder to predict for long-term English Learners with IEPs.
target_learners: High school English Learners, including former, long-term, and late-arriving English Learners
target_learning_goals: High school graduation, college enrollment, and college degree completion
examples: The study found active English Learners need attendance above 95% while former and never English Learners need 90% or higher to be very likely to graduate.
key_sources: Allensworth, E.M., de la Torre, M., Franklin, K., & Xu, J. (2025). Identifying Indicators to Support Educational Attainment for Different Groups of English Learners in High School. (Working Paper). Providence, RI: Annenberg EdExchange. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai25-1241

article_title: 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes
citation: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Satellite data: high-level aggregate measures that lack ground-level context
description: The brief adopts Safir and Dugan's (2021) concept of satellite data to name the kind of data education leaders most often rely on: easily quantified, aggregate measures such as test scores, graduation rates, and attendance. The brief states these data "provide a high-level view but do not provide the context, detail, and nuance" needed to fully understand and respond to student learning needs. The concept organizes the brief's argument for supplementing quantitative measures with qualitative data.
requirements: Should be paired with closer-to-the-ground qualitative sources to gain context, detail, and nuance
constraints: Applies to data that can be easily quantified and analyzed in aggregate
target_learners: all students in systems evaluated mainly through aggregate measures
target_learning_goals: understanding learning needs with sufficient context and nuance
examples: The brief applies the satellite-data label to test scores, graduation rates, and attendance data
key_sources: Jessica Arnold, Julie Webb. (2024). 7 Recommendations for Using Education Data to Support Equitable Learning Outcomes. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED655653

article_title: Del Norte Unified School District: "A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services through Project Cal-Well"
citation: WestEd. (2024). Del Norte Unified School District: A Comprehensive Approach to Mental Health Services Through Project Cal-Well. https://www.wested.org/
title: SAEBRS multi-informant universal mental health screening in DNUSD

District capacity to monitor and respond to screening results

Data-informed allocation of mental health supports
examples: Nearly 11,000 student screenings conducted from fall 2020 through December 2023

citation: Babineau, K., Shah, Z., Jacobs, B., Miller, A., Alvarado, B., Aguirre, N., Fennelly-Atkinson, R., & Young, V. (2025). Building Bridges: Cultivating Interconnectedness for STEM Pathways in San Diego. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/254
title: San Diego STEM Pathways Community Advisory Committee (CAC)
description: The CAC is a cross-sector coalition formed in 2024 to lay the groundwork for regional STEM pathway initiatives. This 14-member committee spans early childhood education, K-12, postsecondary, workforce development, community-based organizations, and philanthropy. Members meet monthly, connect asynchronously between meetings, and have established collaboration principles, engaged learners and industry leaders in co-design, and developed four solution concepts for STEM pathways.

Commitment to long-term, sustainable leadership and transparent partnerships across sectors

article_title: Evidence for Social and Emotional Learning in Schools
citation: Greenberg, M. T. (2023). Evidence for social and emotional learning in schools. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/928.269
title: Use SAFE program design — Sequenced, Active, Focused, Explicit — for effective SEL programming
description: The report states that effective SEL programs utilize four practices represented by the acronym SAFE: programs are "Sequenced", "Active", "Focused", and "Explicit", meaning they involve developmentally coordinated activities, active skill learning, intentional development of personal and social skills, and clearly identified, taught, and practiced skills. This design principle guides selection and design of SEL curricula.

examples: The report cites research indicating effective programs utilize the four SAFE practices, drawing on prior implementation research

article_title: Corequisite Remediation in Mathematics: A Review of First-Year Implementation and Outcomes of Quantway and Statway
citation: Strother, S., & Klipple, K. (2019). Corequisite remediation in math: A review of first-year implementation and outcomes of Quantway and Statway. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://carnegiemathpathways.org/reports/
title: Same-faculty cohort pairing of college-level and corequisite courses
description: All six implementing institutions delivered the paired courses as a cohort, with one instructor teaching both the college-level and the developmental-level course to the same group of students. Faculty reported that this continuity supported student comfort, consistent social support, and continuity of pedagogical approaches, and let them make ongoing adjustments to content and timeline. As the report prints it, "All institutions used a cohort model for course delivery, with the same faculty member teaching each of the paired courses (college-level and developmental-level) to the same group of students." Faculty at the two multi-section institutions also met weekly and visited one another's classrooms to improve strategies during the term.
requirements: The same faculty member teaches both paired courses to the same group of students
constraints: The report states that since no other strategies were attempted, the effect of using the cohort strategy versus other strategies needs further investigation
target_learners: Developmental math students in corequisite course pairs at community colleges and four-year institutions
target_learning_goals: Persistence and success in college-level quantitative reasoning or statistics
examples: Faculty at the two multi-section institutions held weekly meetings and classroom visits to adjust lessons, homework, and exams throughout the term

article_title: Sustainable Strategies for Funding Teacher Residencies: Lessons from California
citation: Yun, C., & DeMoss, K. (2020). Sustainable strategies for funding teacher residencies: Lessons from California. Palo Alto, CA: Learning Policy Institute. http://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/strategies-funding-teacher-residencies-california
title: Sanger STaR integrated two-semester curriculum: eleven courses consolidated into two yearlong integrated courses, saving residents roughly $4,000
description: Fresno State faculty and Sanger Unified leadership redesigned the STaR residency curriculum from three semesters with eleven separate courses into two yearlong integrated courses, one spanning pedagogy content and one covering curriculum and subject-matter instruction. Faculty teams collaborated for over a year, using classroom-based inquiry cycles around "real-time puzzles of practice" as a common structure. "For the 25 STaR residents, the two-semester model was beneficial in more ways than saving an entire semester’s worth of time and roughly $4,000 in tuition," including a free summer to earn money and no-cost course materials.
requirements: Sustained faculty collaboration across expertise areas (literacy, special education, mathematics, science, culturally and linguistically sustaining pedagogy) and alignment with district professional development initiatives
constraints: The redesign responded to Sanger's specific district initiatives, such as earlier introduction of inclusion and differentiation strategies; the report presents it as one local design, not a general model
target_learners: Multiple-subject teacher residency candidates, including those seeking bilingual certification
target_learning_goals: Deeper, more coherent learning through integrated coursework
Modeling integrated lesson planning and teaching for residents' own practice
examples: The previous model's summer, fall, and spring course lists were consolidated so that two yearlong courses replaced eleven separate courses, with clinical work continuing yearlong in the classroom.

article_title: Mapping artificial intelligence integration in higher education: A systematic review using the FACETS and SAMR frameworks
citation: AlSheikh MH, Zaini R, ALmulhem MA and Ahmad S (2026). Mapping artificial intelligence integration in higher education: a systematic review using the FACETS and SAMR frameworks. Front. Educ. 11:1871468. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1871468
title: SAMR model of technology integration levels (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition)
description: The SAMR model categorizes the depth of technology integration in educational settings across four levels. The review defines them: "Substitution: AI does the same task as previous methods"; "Augmentation: AI enhances and extends traditional methods"; "Modification: AI alters the nature of learning and assessment tasks"; and "Redefinition: AI enables tasks and experiences previously impossible." It was selected for its widespread use in evaluating levels of technology integration and used to classify each included AI application.
requirements: Raters must classify each AI-supported learning activity into one of the four levels during analysis
constraints: The review states SAMR effectively categorizes technology integration levels but may oversimplify complex pedagogical interactions
target_learners: undergraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: evaluating the pedagogical depth of AI-supported learning activities
examples: Examples in the review include automated anatomical OSPE grading as Substitution, adaptive quizzing as Augmentation, a ChatGPT-flipped classroom as Modification, and an AI co-created biomedical informatics course as Redefinition
key_sources: AlSheikh MH, Zaini R, ALmulhem MA and Ahmad S (2026). Mapping artificial intelligence integration in higher education: a systematic review using the FACETS and SAMR frameworks. Front. Educ. 11:1871468. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1871468

article_title: EduGuard: A Safe RAG-Based LLM Tutor for Programming Education
citation: S M Asif Hossain, Ruksat Khan Shayoni, M. F. Mridha, and Jungpil Shin. (2026). EduGuard: A Safe RAG-Based LLM Tutor for Programming Education. arXiv preprint arXiv:2607.15738. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15738
title: Safe GenAI tutoring requires explicit pedagogical control, evidence verification, and deployment safeguards, not only retrieval or stronger prompting
description: The article argues that grounding and prompting alone cannot ensure safe tutoring because retrieved context may still leak solutions and self-checks share generator failure modes. It concludes that "safe GenAI tutoring requires not only retrieval or strong prompting, but explicit pedagogical control, evidence verification, and deployment safeguards." Deployment safeguards include instructor oversight, opt-out options, de-identification, retention limits, and clear warnings that the system provides formative support rather than grading decisions.
requirements: Explicit pedagogical strategy policy, a claim-level verifier separate from the generator, and instructor oversight during student-facing use
constraints: The authors state the system should not be treated as ready for autonomous deployment
Leakage policy is partly contextual; what is allowed in one course may be disallowed in another
target_learners: undergraduate students in introductory programming courses
target_learning_goals: safe and integrity-preserving use of AI tutoring support
examples: EduGuard implements the principle by regenerating responses that fail claim verification and returning refusal-with-guidance when a second draft also fails

article_title: Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics
citation: Zachery Quince and Emily Faulconer. (2026). Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00651-w
title: SAMR as a metric of constructive-alignment depth for GenAI use in assessment
description: The article positions the SAMR framework (Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition) not as a taxonomy of technology use but as a measure of how deeply GenAI integration preserves or bypasses constructive alignment. It states that "the SAMR framework is uniquely appropriate because it focuses on the functional behaviour change in the learning task, distinguishing between use as a passive cognitive shortcut (substitution) or as a cognitive partner for deep inquiry (redefinition)". Constructive alignment provides the baseline for assessment validity, and authentic assessment serves as the design intervention that fosters evaluative judgement so students critically engage with GenAI rather than offload cognitive effort.
requirements: Assessment tasks must be aligned with learning outcomes and activities so that SAMR level can be read as depth of alignment rather than tool frequency
constraints: The article cautions against viewing SAMR as a simple hierarchy; each level can be pedagogically appropriate depending on learning goals, and the mapping is context-dependent across disciplines and assessment types
target_learners: undergraduate STEM students
target_learning_goals: authentic demonstration of disciplinary reasoning under GenAI-available conditions
examples: Student declarations were mapped to SAMR levels: Learning and Formatting aligned with substitution/augmentation, Doing Task with modification/redefinition, and Feedback spanned all four levels
key_sources: Zachery Quince and Emily Faulconer. (2026). Student GenAI use under changing institutional policies: a mixed-methods case study in undergraduate physics. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00651-w

article_title: SafeTutors: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems
citation: Rima Hazra, Bikram Ghuku, Ilona Marchenko, Yaroslava Tokarieva, Sayan Layek, Somnath Banerjee, Julia Stoyanovich, Mykola Pechenizkiy. (2026). SAFETUTORS: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.17373
title: SAFETUTORS benchmark: 3,135 single-turn instances and 2,820 multi-turn tutoring sequences across three STEM domains
description: SAFETUTORS is a benchmark for joint safety and pedagogical evaluation of AI tutors in mathematics, physics, and chemistry. It comprises "3,135 single-turn instances and 2,820 multi-turn tutoring sequences constructed via crescendo-based escalation", with multi-turn conversations spanning 5-8 turns. Data was built from seed questions in MathDial and CAMEL-AI, filtered with GPT-5.2, and validated through three human annotation stages reaching Fleiss' kappa of 0.82, 0.74, and 0.69 across stages, with 91.3% of instances receiving consistent final labels after adjudication.
requirements: Human validation through expert annotation to ensure pedagogical validity, conversational coherence, and alignment with intended risk categories
constraints: Covers three STEM domains only (physics, chemistry, mathematics); automated harm scoring is done by LLM judges with majority voting, verified against human labeling on a stratified sample with Cohen's kappa = 0.76
target_learners: Students in mathematics, physics, and chemistry at varied difficulty levels
target_learning_goals: Scaffolded problem solving, misconception repair, and mastery of STEM learning objectives
examples: Multi-turn conversations begin with a legitimate scientific problem and student utterances progressively steer the tutor toward a specific risk category

article_title: Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate students as partners in generative AI innovation
citation: Lo S, Lea T, Mavromoustakos A, Joseph B, Yii M, Exintaris B, Karunaratne N, Pearson DL, Ritchie T, Yuriev E and Pyun J (2026) Co-creating custom GPTs: an autoethnographic study of undergraduate students as partners in generative AI innovation. Front. Educ. 11:1818781. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1818781
title: Students-as-partners framework extended to GenAI tool co-creation
description: The students-as-partners (SaP) framework positions students and staff in a "collaborative, reciprocal process through which all participants have the opportunity to contribute equally, although not necessarily in the same ways, to curricular or pedagogical conceptualization, decision-making, implementation, investigation, or analysis". The article applies SaP values of respect, reciprocity, and shared responsibility to co-creating custom GPTs, arguing that co-creation with GenAI can extend the SaP paradigm to include GenAI tools, with students as co-creators rather than passive users or risks.

target_learning_goals: digital literacies and critical understanding of AI
examples: Five students and five academics co-created seven cGPTs across six units, with students adopting roles as content curators, builders, testers, evaluators, and data analysts

article_title: SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis
citation: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413
title: SAVVY interactive visual analytics system with Concept, Group, and Individual modules
description: SAVVY is an interactive visual analytics system that integrates visual and auditory attention to support top-down exploration of student attention variations in video-based learning. It comprises three coordinated visualization modules linked by a shared timeline: a Concept Module presenting course content structure and concept-level attention distribution, a Group Module visualizing group attention trends alongside audiovisual information density, and an Individual Module providing multi-temporal-resolution attention trajectories. The modules incorporate "course content structure, audiovisual information density, and attentional resource allocation," enabling teachers to analyze causes of attention fluctuations and inform instructional video improvement through a top-down workflow from course overview to individual verification.
requirements: A preprocessed multimodal brain dataset with quantified attention levels and processed instructional videos supplying course structure and information density
constraints: The system addresses video-side factors an instructor can control and does not model learner-side factors such as fatigue, mind-wandering, sleep, or prior familiarity
target_learners: teachers and course instructors revising instructional videos for video-based learning
target_learning_goals: locating when and why student attention declines and determining which instructional video content needs revision
examples: In Case 1, E1 used the Concept Module to screen concepts, the Group Module to discover anomalous information density and attention contributions, and the Individual Module to verify causes of attention decline in a convolutional neural networks course
key_sources: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413

article_title: SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis
citation: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413
title: Six design requirements organized by concept, group, and individual analysis objects for attention visualization
description: From a preliminary study with four education experts, the authors derived six design requirements (R1-R6) categorized by three analysis objects: the course concept, the student group, and the individual student. The Concept category analyzes attention from the course structure for rapid screening and preliminary attribution; the Group category focuses on temporal attention trends and audiovisual instructional design; and the Individual category centers on "each student's detailed attention trajectory and audiovisual attention allocation." The decomposition matches the experts' agreed top-down workflow from overall course structure to specific causes of attention fluctuations.
requirements: Accurate extraction of concepts and their relationships as a prerequisite for helping teachers review the overall course structure
constraints: Group aggregated results may mask individual differences, as attention patterns observed at the group level may not hold consistently across individual students
target_learners: teachers and course instructors analyzing pilot-cohort attention data
target_learning_goals: locating low-engagement segments and diagnosing audiovisual instructional design deficiencies in instructional videos
examples: R2 aggregates attention distribution by concept with concept importance shown via occurrence frequency and duration; R5 supports switching between multiple temporal resolutions for individual trajectories
key_sources: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413

article_title: SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis
citation: Shixian Zhou, Minghuan Shen, Xiaolin Wen, Zijun Qiu, Yongliang Jiang, Xiangyang Wu, Fei Wu, Yong Wang, and Zhiguang Zhou. (2026). SAVVY: Student Attention Visualization for Video-based Learning Analysis. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.29413
title: Content-derived visual and auditory information density metrics grounded in LC4MP
description: Grounded in the Limited Capacity Model of Motivated Mediated Message Processing (LC4MP), SAVVY quantifies information density of both visual and auditory channels per slide-transition-induced event segment. Visual density combines edge density of image regions (detected with Mask R-CNN), average normalized IDF surprisal of slide text (detected with DBNet), weighted by region area ratios; auditory density uses the entropy of the narration's word distribution divided by narration duration, plus semantic similarity between slide text and transcript to capture cross-channel redundancy. The authors caution these are "content-derived proxy indicators" describing the presented content itself, not learners' internal cognitive states.
requirements: Instructional videos with slides and narration transcripts for region detection, transcription, and per-segment computation
constraints: The metrics describe the presented content itself, not learners' internal cognitive states, nor the amount of information each learner actually and selectively takes in
target_learners: teachers assessing the appropriateness of audiovisual design in instructional videos
target_learning_goals: diagnosing whether visual or auditory information density contributes to low student attention
examples: Edge density was chosen for image regions because instructional graphics are mostly structured diagrams composed of lines, boundaries, arrows, grids, and contours

title: Seven sample prompts scaffolding collaborative ChatGPT interaction in creative problem-solving

Access to ChatGPT during the collaboration phase

article_title: Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering -Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI-
citation: Riichiro Mizoguchi, Tomoki Aburatani, Kento Koike, Machi Shimmei. (2026). Vibe Compiler: A Research-Logic Synthesis Tool That Runs without Prompt Engineering —Toward Enhancing Metacognition for Sustaining Agency in the Age of Generative AI—. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05545
title: Synthesis–Analysis Reciprocity Model: intellectual construction as a mutual-constraint loop between Synthesis and Analysis
description: The model decomposes intellectual construction into Synthesis, which selects and combines known logical components according to a purpose, and Analysis, which critically evaluates the artifact against objective criteria. Its defining feature is mutual constraint: "the output of Analysis is not consumed as an evaluation result; it flows back immediately as a constraint on the next Synthesis." The model is developed as a dual-layer structure — a learner layer (arithmetic problem posing, reading comprehension) and a researcher layer (research-logic type checking) — sharing one reciprocity mechanism with only the Analysis mapping swapped out. The authors position it against introspective models such as reflection and self-regulated learning, which lack an external objective indicator.
requirements: A reference solution must be presentable for a given artifact (AI as an Oracle), whose errors are woven into the design as occasions for reverse Analysis

description: The Safety Gap is the article's central concept: the divergence between the polished output a learner produces with generative AI and their ability to independently reproduce or verify that output. description: SAIL is an AI literacy framework developed from a Delphi study that structures learning as a scaffolded pathway through competency levels applicable across ages and educational stages. The framework is explicitly age agnostic: higher levels suit older learners, but "Level 1 concepts were appropriate (indeed, essential) to all age groups", with educators adapting delivery to context. Educators developing their own AI literacy

citation: Lauren E. Margulieux · Brendan D. Calandra · Bryan Cox. (2026). Online professional development to support K‑12 teachers' computer science integration. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10640-z
title: SAMR framework for levels of technology-enhanced learning activities
description: The Substitution, Augmentation, Modification, Redefinition (SAMR) framework describes differences in the quality of activities afforded by technological tools. In the first two levels, activities are "fundamentally the same as the original activities": Substitution uses technology for the same activity, perhaps more efficiently, while Augmentation adds something that could not have been done without it. In Modification and Redefinition, technology qualitatively changes the activity, with Redefinition incorporating new tasks that would have been impossible without technology. The MICRO PD drew its example activities primarily from the last two levels, framing programming as teaching the computer to complete a task.
requirements: No level of SAMR is right or wrong; the appropriate level depends on a teacher's teaching and learning goals.
constraints: The authors did not expect that teachers' applications of the PD would necessarily always align with the higher levels of SAMR.
target_learners: K-12 teachers integrating computing into non-CS classrooms
target_learning_goals: designing technology-enhanced learning activities at appropriate integration levels
examples: The PD framed creating a computer program as teaching the computer to complete a task, which the authors say pushes activities to at least the Modification level.
